knowledge.question: Should I promote my show as a beginner?
knowledge.answer: Levi says be strategic. Don't promote your show if you only have five different products, and as a complete beginner he wouldn't recommend promoting it.

knowledge.question: How do I give buyers store credit or giveaways?
knowledge.answer: Levi does store credit giveaways, and says you just make a coupon. He also sends envelopes with giveaways, coupons and store credit as marketing.

knowledge.question: Should I be on Whatnot or TikTok Shop?
knowledge.answer: Levi thinks every business should implement live shopping one way or another. He sees TikTok Shop as more for brand building, so brands on Amazon not using it are leaving money on the table. For a normal reseller with $50–$200, he says start on Whatnot.

knowledge.question: What should I do with Amazon or Walmart returns I'm stuck with?
knowledge.answer: Sell them on Whatnot. Levi says get your money back and move on, because you don't want to hold on to dead stock.

knowledge.question: Why am I profitable but not seeing cash in my bank account?
knowledge.answer: Levi says it's usually one of two things: you're reinvesting everything and buying a lot with longer lead times, or you're not selling through your inventory. For example, 100,000 units sitting in a warehouse, like he has, sold at $4 each is $400,000 just sitting in inventory. To realize those profits, you have to sell through the inventory.

knowledge.question: What should I sell on Whatnot if I only have about $500?
knowledge.answer: Levi says he'd go to storage auctions on sites like StorageTreasures and buy a $10 to $100 unit, keeping it under $100 so you have money for shipping supplies. A $50 unit could have 20 boxes with 20 items each: 400 items at about 40 cents apiece. Start everything at $1 on Whatnot, sell it in one night, and compound quickly. That's how he started.

knowledge.question: How do I make sure I'm getting a good deal on a liquidation pallet?
knowledge.answer: Take everything out of the pallet and count it yourself so you know the real unit count and price per unit. Levi's friend bought a pallet quoted at $2.30 a unit, counted it, and found more items than the liquidator said, so it was really $2 a unit. Liquidators who buy manifested loads often only have an estimate.

knowledge.question: Should I go straight to buying truckloads or contracts with big retailers?
knowledge.answer: Levi says no. Your local liquidator likely has a contract to take 10 or even 100 trucks a month, which ties up a lot of cash and warehouse space you probably don't have. Build a relationship with them and your price per unit will keep dropping. Retailer contracts with Target or Amazon only make sense at high scale with a huge warehouse, because you have to take everything they send, even two truckloads of plastic trays.

knowledge.question: Are online or estate auctions a good inventory source for Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: They can be a way to start small, Levi says, but you end up handpicking too many individual items. Whatnot works best with a very wide catalog, and liquidation pallets already come mixed, in quantity, cheap, and hopefully good quality.

knowledge.question: Is wholesale or retail arbitrage better than liquidation for Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi doesn't think so. He asks why buy wholesale when liquidation has higher margins and higher returns. Retail arbitrage, like buying Adidas or Nike shoes to resell, has lower margins and lower returns too. For him, liquidation has the highest return and profit margin on Whatnot right now.

knowledge.question: What category should I start selling in on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi used to recommend beauty because it's easy to find and small to ship. Once you're past that phase, he says sell everything and go as wide as possible. Build trust in one category, then expand into others so you get more returning buyers. That's why he likes mixed liquidation pallets.

knowledge.question: Why is selling only cheap items bad for my Whatnot business?
knowledge.answer: Low-ticket items take longer to sell, which hurts your sell-through rate. Levi bought 2,500 cheap items that took four or five days to sell (longer if a streamer called out), meaning five days of labor while he kept buying. By comparison, 300 high-ticket items with about a $30 average sale price sold in one six-hour show: one day of labor and the profit in one day. Low ticket has good margins, but you want a blend.

knowledge.question: Should I run a dedicated big-item show?
knowledge.answer: Levi ran bigger items in a 'big item show' once a week. When he stopped for all of January, buyers kept asking when the big item show was coming back. Running or displaying big-ticket items also attracts more people into your low-ticket shows.

knowledge.question: How do I get more returning buyers on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Add more categories and keep testing new ones instead of selling the same thing. In December and January Levi sold mostly lunch boxes and book bags, and buyers said they already had five or ten. After adding categories and big items, his returning buyer rate went to nearly 50% in February (about 50 of every 100 buyers), compared with 70-80% new buyers before January.

knowledge.question: When should I start buying case packs for Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi doesn't recommend case pack loads until you're moving more volume. Case packs can bring your buy cost under $1 per unit, and Whatnot lets you sell 1,000 of one product fast and cheap where Amazon or eBay can't. Don't sell it all in one show; blend it in with your mixed pallets across days and weeks. You can sell 1,000 of one item once you have a buyer base, sell daily, and run many streams.

knowledge.question: What should I do if a product's price keeps dropping because I run it too often?
knowledge.answer: Take a break from it. Levi bought 3,000 Altec speakers and ran them every day; they started at $45 and dropped to $15-20 because it seemed everyone already had one. If too many people have it, wait a week and run it again, and you get a fresh set of buyers who haven't seen it and higher prices.

knowledge.question: Why does consistent, good-quality inventory help my prices?
knowledge.answer: Buyers can't feel quality through a screen, but once they receive a good product, prices spike about two weeks later as they tell friends. Levi saw this with high-quality canvas tote bags that cost $15 at Target and sold for $5 on his show. Consistent inventory builds trust in you and the product.

knowledge.question: How many units do I need to sell to hit $50K a month?
knowledge.answer: Use Levi's simple formula: take $50,000, divide by 30 days, then divide by your average sale price to get your exact number of units per day. For reference, he sells low-ticket items bought for $1-3. His average buy cost is $1.80 against an average sale price of around $6, a 3x, and prep fees run about 50 cents a unit.

knowledge.question: Should I pay someone who promises to get me a TikTok account manager?
knowledge.answer: No. Levi says anyone selling you a TikTok account manager is scamming you and lying to you. Even with access to top TikTok managers, his team can't get beginners set up: managers don't want to deal with you unless you're doing more than about $65-75K a month in sales. He says that if his team can't do it, no one else can either.

knowledge.question: Is TikTok a good platform for a beginner seller?
knowledge.answer: Not usually. Levi tells his students that if you're a beginner with less than $5,000 in sales, or only $5,000 to your name, TikTok is not the best platform to be on. Without roughly $65-75K a month in sales, you won't get manager support on TikTok.

knowledge.question: How fast do I get paid on Whatnot compared to TikTok?
knowledge.answer: Once you unlock instant payouts on Whatnot, you get paid the same day or the next day. Levi's example: sell 2,000 units in one day at even a $6 average sale price and you get paid about 13 grand the next day. On TikTok, getting instant payouts typically means you need an account manager, need to be in JBP, and need to be doing a lot of sales. He says few platforms pay that fast, and that's what drives growth in this business.

knowledge.question: What printer should I use for Whatnot shipping labels?
knowledge.answer: Levi uses a roll thermal label printer that cost about $200; he has three of them and they've printed over 100,000 labels. He uses it for both the item numbers and the shipping labels, and says it's worth the investment over printer ink. You have to download the printer's driver from the manufacturer's website for Mac or PC, then print from your laptop with Command+P.

knowledge.question: How do I print all the shipping labels for a Whatnot show?
knowledge.answer: Go to Seller Hub, then Shipments, and pick the show you're working on; shipments are divided by show. Select all the orders (he selects all 250 at once), click Generate Labels, then Export Shipping Labels and view/print the PDF. Levi recommends using a laptop and printing everything at once, including packing slips, before anyone starts packing.

knowledge.question: What is a scan sheet on Whatnot and when do I need it?
knowledge.answer: A scan sheet is what you give the USPS driver or the post office clerk so all your packages get scanned in at once. You can only create it the same day you print the labels, before 12 a.m. Levi recommends using it when dropping off a lot of packages, because USPS hates volume and if you bring more than 20 boxes every day they'll probably start to dislike you. His new driver brings a scanner, which improved their on-time shipment rate.

knowledge.question: How should I organize labels before my team starts packing?
knowledge.answer: Once all the labels print, cut them and split them into piles: ground, priority, first-class mail and giveaways. That way shippers can do all the priority orders together using priority mail boxes, which means fewer mistakes like putting a ground label on a Priority Mail box. Giveaways and first-class mail get done at the end, with one person just shipping out the stickers.

knowledge.question: How do I make sure the right item goes to the right buyer?
knowledge.answer: When you have multiple shows, Levi recommends checking at least one order against the video receipt. Type the order number into the shipments search, expand it, and watch the video receipt to see the item sold, then match it to the numbered item on the shelf and the label. If they match, you know you're working the correct show. Items are kept in numbered order on shelves so they're easy to find.

knowledge.question: Should I include packing slips in Whatnot orders?
knowledge.answer: Yes. Levi says packing slips cost less than a penny each and many buyers buy from lots of shows, so the slip tells them what the package is, especially since USPS can deliver today's order before one from three days ago. They also make it easy on shippers: once the slips are printed, nobody has to look at the laptop again, they just match the number on the slip, grab the item and pack. Not everyone on the team needs to be tech-savvy; one person prints and the rest pack.

knowledge.question: What's the fastest way to pick a large bundle order?
knowledge.answer: Levi puts the box on the ground and drops the items in as he follows the list of numbers, instead of carrying the box around. Then bring it to the table, bubble wrap only if needed, close it, label it and weigh it. He picked a 40-item, 17 lb order in about 3 minutes this way, and says this method helped a friend go from 16 hours with eight employees to shipping 1,000 items in about 3 hours with three to four workers.

knowledge.question: Should I sell fragile items on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi stays away from items that take a long time to pack. Fragile items need lots of bubble wrap and take longer, so if you sell them your buy cost needs to be low and your profit high. Most of what he sells, like squishies in plastic packaging or backpacks, can be dropped straight into a box or poly mailer with no bubble wrap.

knowledge.question: When should I use Priority Mail vs Ground on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi uses Priority Mail for anything from 1 to 5 lb and Ground for anything over 5 lb. He says USPS shipping is very cheap per pound between 5 and 20 lb, and it's only after 20 lb that they start charging a lot per pound. Ground orders can't go in a Priority Mail box, so they go in a brown box or a poly mailer.

knowledge.question: How do I downgrade a big order to a flat rate box on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: If a big order fits in a large flat rate box, go back to the shipment on the laptop, edit it, choose Large Flat Rate and reprint the label. Levi says it's completely free and doesn't count toward your weekly label-change allowance, because the customer already paid more than the $9.21 a large flat rate box costs. He fit a 40-item, 17 lb ground order into one flat rate box this way.

knowledge.question: Is it worth paying out of pocket to split a big order into two boxes?
knowledge.answer: Yes, in Levi's view. In his example, two large flat rate boxes cost $18.42 but the customer paid about $14 in shipping, so he paid around $5 out of pocket on a $135, 40-item order. He says keeping a big buyer in your show is worth far more than $5, because they're also bidding and pushing prices up on other items.

knowledge.question: What box sizes should I use for Whatnot orders?
knowledge.answer: Levi uses 18x12x8 boxes because they have the same cubic inches as a 12x12x12 box (1,728), so they cost the same. He keeps small poly mailers for one-item orders, which you can buy cheaply on Amazon, plus Priority Mail boxes and tape. He notes one-item orders cost a bit more to pack because you're using your own poly mailers.

knowledge.question: How can I do product research on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Look at what other sellers are winning with: their products, their listings and their average sale price. Levi says that's product research right there, and it's not spying because it's all public information. The tool he uses grabs that public data and organizes it so you can track it over time.

knowledge.question: How do I set up 'buy two, next three free shipping' on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Instead of charging 1 lb for items that weigh about a pound, Levi charges 15 oz. The first item costs about $7-7.70 in shipping and the second about $2.21, the difference up to $9.21. Items three, four and five are free because the box stays in the 1-5 lb range at $9.21. If they only buy two items you can still change the label to 80 oz at the same price.

knowledge.question: Should I put a max bundle size on my shipping profile?
knowledge.answer: Levi says it depends on your size. If you're new and can invest in boxes, keep a max of five and take advantage of the Priority Mail boxes. As a bigger seller, he now removes the max and lets Whatnot handle the weight: anything over 5 lb ships ground, and buyers pay roughly $1-2 on the sixth item and about 45-75 cents per item after that. With a max of five, the sixth item starts a new bundle at about $7 shipping again, so most buyers don't open another bundle.

knowledge.question: Why did Levi stop doing 'buy two, next eight free shipping'?
knowledge.answer: With buy two, next eight free, they were paying a lot of the shipping cost out of pocket for anything at 5 lb or higher when adjusting labels. Switching back to buy two, next three free with no max bundle size passes more of the cost to the customer. Average sale prices barely changed and customers haven't complained, because shipping per extra item is still very cheap.

knowledge.question: Is there a point where shipping gets expensive for big bundles?
knowledge.answer: Levi noticed that around the 20th to 23rd item in a bundle, the per-item shipping charge jumps to roughly $1-3, up to $3.83 for one customer, which he thinks is USPS charging more for heavier boxes. So he planned to test a max of 20 items per bundle instead of unlimited. He points out few buyers go past 20 items anyway: in his data only one bought 25.

knowledge.question: Should I do big giveaways on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi recommends bigger giveaways only for bigger sellers with low buy costs and low labor cost per unit. He started doing $50 bundle giveaways and his viewership nearly doubled, from around 90-100 viewers to a peak of 210. Note a $50 bundle doesn't cost him $50 since he buys at a percentage of Target retail. For small sellers he says keep giveaways small and scale up slowly.

knowledge.question: Can I afford to pay for shipping and do big giveaways at the same time?
knowledge.answer: Levi says it's one or the other because doing both gets very expensive. He chose to pass more shipping cost to customers so he could fund better giveaways, which bring in new buyers. His goal was to raise his new-buyer rate after his returning buyer rate had shifted to about 50% daily.

knowledge.question: How do I figure out the best shipping setup for my shows?
knowledge.answer: Keep testing. Levi says there's no information out there on Whatnot shipping, so he finds these patterns by checking real customer bundles and the per-item shipping charges, then testing changes like maxing at 20 items. He also watches whether changes affect average sale price.

knowledge.question: How should I approach suppliers when networking?
knowledge.answer: Be yourself. Levi says suppliers, and people in general, love genuine people; they don't want to be sold, and they don't want it to feel like it's all business. Don't just go around asking how much for this and how much for that. Talk about yourself, talk about your business and tell them what you do.

knowledge.question: Can I get a TikTok account manager as a small seller?
knowledge.answer: Probably not. Levi says he could lie to promote his coaching and promise to get you a manager, but he won't. Their managers told them they hate working with small sellers. The managers are paid salary, not commission or bonuses, so they put their time and energy where it's easiest and shows the most GMV for their portfolio. Some of Levi's friends have the same managers and don't get responses, while he does, because it comes down to politics and how much money you make.

knowledge.question: How do I stay on good terms with a TikTok account manager?
knowledge.answer: Figure things out yourself first. Levi says managers dislike small sellers who ask too many questions, and they like that he and his brother solve problems on their own before reaching out. When there's a problem, try to work it out before contacting them, and keep your requests minimal.

knowledge.question: What can I do if my TikTok Shop gets banned?
knowledge.answer: Don't let one ban kill your business. Levi says you can have five shops under one LLC, and if one shop gets cooked, you can make another shop under a different LLC. You don't need a rep, and you don't need a TikTok guru telling you otherwise.

knowledge.question: What shipping boxes should I order as a beginner?
knowledge.answer: Levi says order a large flat rate box and a large shipping box and don't worry about anything else. A large flat rate box can ship up to 70 lb for $9.21, so it's great for liquids or heavy batteries. A large shipping box, or any box that doesn't say flat rate, is for 1 to 5 lb priority mail. Even if a buyer gets one small item, ship it in the same box; when your team only has to make one box, shipping is much more efficient.

knowledge.question: Which shipping settings should I pick in the Whatnot app?
knowledge.answer: In the app (not the laptop), choose priority mail for 1 to 5 lb and priority mail for anything over 5 lb. Levi says this saves beginners a headache because you can always downgrade to ground or flat rate later. He also recommends always setting a max bundle size with a custom shipping profile.

knowledge.question: How do I set my shipping profile so buyers get priority mail on the first item?
knowledge.answer: Set the first item at 71 to 75 oz and every item after that at 1 oz, with a max bundle (Levi uses 10). Anything under 1 lb is ground shipping, so a 15 oz or 8 oz first item puts single-item buyers on slow ground. With this setup, a single-item buyer pays $9.21 and gets priority mail, and every item after is free shipping. If a single item weighs 3 lb, it ships as 4 lb priority without overcharges.

knowledge.question: Will buyers still pay $9.21 shipping on just one item?
knowledge.answer: Levi's results say yes. He had 100 one-item orders in one show at $9.21 because buyers are still getting steals under retail. With the old 8+8 or 15+15 oz setup, the first item cost about $4.50 to $7.50 and the second about $1 to $3, which still added up to $9.21. Now buyers just pay once upfront and see free shipping immediately on the second item, which encourages them to stay and keep buying.

knowledge.question: Why does Levi prefer priority mail over ground shipping?
knowledge.answer: Faster shipping gets better reviews, and customers blame you for slow delivery. Levi got a bad review for a 5-day delivery from New Jersey to Washington even on priority; with ground it would have been worse. Charging $9.21 upfront also stopped his team from spending 20 to 40 cents on poly mailers for $1 one-item ground orders that put him in the red. He'd rather spend about 90 cents on a box for buyers who fill their bundles.

knowledge.question: Can I cut down a shipping box to make it smaller?
knowledge.answer: Yes, but only with a regular priority mail shipping box, never a flat rate box. Flat rate boxes of any kind (small, medium, padded, flat) can't be altered. A box that doesn't say flat rate can be cut down from the top, for example from a 12x12x12 to the size you need, which saves you on boxes.

knowledge.question: How do I switch an order to a flat rate box in Shipments?
knowledge.answer: Before generating the label, open the shipment, go to edit shipping information, choose use flat rate box and pick large, then update the label. It won't charge you anything because flat rate is a downgrade from priority mail. Levi doesn't recommend doing this on every order though, because you have to toggle it and reprint each label, which takes time.

knowledge.question: Should I tell buyers how many items I'm selling in the show?
knowledge.answer: Yes. Levi tells customers they'll run 500 items that day and puts it in the listing description. People who show up at item 400 know there aren't many chances left to fill their bundle, so it gets competitive, especially with sudden death. His team sees a spike in prices in the last 50 to 100 items as people try to fill their free shipping, since a full 10-item bundle at $9.21 is only 92 cents of shipping per item.

knowledge.question: Should a beginner copy the $9.21 upfront shipping setup?
knowledge.answer: Levi gives it as a disclaimer: as a beginner you can do what he used to do, like 8+8 oz, or 15+15 oz for electronics with a max bundle of five. But he also says to protect your reviews by charging $9.21 upfront for priority mail, especially during the holidays, and he doesn't plan to go back. Base your max bundle size on your average item size; shirts, for example, easily fit 10 in one box.
